draft.title: Pork and Green Mango Soup

ingredients.note: Mentioned as a side to serve with the soup.
Cut into small chunks with bone left on for flavor.
For blanching the pork.
For searing pork and onions.
For initial boil and main broth base.
Divided use: cooked in broth base and sliced thin for finishing.
Must be sour green mangoes, cut into 1-inch strips.
Chopped for garnish/finishing.
Cut into small pieces.

steps.text: Cook the rice to serve with the finished soup.
Chop the pork ribs into small chunks, keeping the bones attached.

why.text: Leaving the bone on adds extra richness and depth to the broth.
why.quote: you want the porks with the bone on them 'cause the bone gives a little bit more flavor to the broth

steps.text: Place pork pieces in a pot of salted water, bring to a rapid boil briefly, then drain completely and rinse off scum and blood.

why.text: Blanching removes impurities so the broth stays clear and clean-tasting.
why.quote: you want to get rid of all the blood and the scum and all the gunk that comes off of the bone that adds a weird flavor to this soup and makes it a little cloudy I don't like those extra proteins and collagens and all that stuff floating around I like crystal clear broth

steps.text: Heat oil in a pot or pan until hot (test heat by inserting a wooden chopstick; oil should bubble around it). Sear the pork chunks until golden brown on all sides.
Add cracked black pepper, then pour in the fish sauce. Let it sizzle for about 30 seconds until the fish sauce reduces slightly and the pepper releases its aroma.
Add chopped onions and stir-fry, scraping up the browned bits stuck to the bottom of the pan, until translucent.
Add water to create the broth base, return the seared pork pieces to the pot, and simmer for 30 minutes to 1 hour until tender.

dials.effect: pork becomes soft and easy to chew

steps.text: While the pork simmers, slice sour green mangoes into 1-inch strips, slice white onions into thin strips, chop green onions, and chop cilantro.

why.text: White onions are used because they are less sweet, balancing the sour green mangoes.
why.quote: slice up white onions 'cause I don't like onions to be a little too sweet in this soup 'cause there's a fruit component and the fruits are a sweet and sour

steps.text: When the pork is tender, add the green mango strips to the pot and simmer for 5 to 10 minutes until slightly softened.

why.text: Cooking softens the hard raw mango and releases its sour flavor into the soup.
why.quote: raw mangoes it's very crunchy and hard you just want to cook it down so that I release it sourness and blends all the flavor together

steps.text: Stir in the freshly sliced white onions, cilantro, and green onions just before removing from heat.
Ladle soup over cooked rice and garnish with sliced chili peppers if desired.

notes: Corrected dictation error 'fish house tries' to 'fish sauce dries'.
Corrected dictation error 'reese's it's aroma' to 'releases its aroma'.
Reordered the ingredient slicing (mangoes, onions, herbs) to occur while the pork simmers, prior to adding them to the pot.

questions.quote: cut up pork ribs into tiny little chunks
questions.question: How many pounds of pork ribs should be used for this recipe?
questions.why_it_matters: Using too little meat yields a thin broth, while too much overpowers the soup ratio.
questions.suggestion: 2 pounds pork spare ribs or baby back ribs

questions.question: How much water should be added for the soup broth base?
questions.why_it_matters: Too much water dilutes the fish sauce and pork flavor; too little makes it overly concentrated.

questions.quote: put your fish sauce in... first you add your pepper then your fish sauce
questions.question: How much fish sauce and black pepper should be added during searing?
questions.why_it_matters: Fish sauce provides the primary saltiness; getting the wrong amount will ruin the seasoning.
questions.suggestion: 3 tablespoons fish sauce and 1/2 teaspoon freshly cracked black pepper

questions.quote: add water to the soup I see add water and then you put the pork pieces back in
questions.question: Were the pork pieces removed from the pan while searing the onions, or did they stay in the pot?
questions.why_it_matters: Leaving the pork in while searing onions can overcrowd the pan and prevent proper onion softening.
questions.suggestion: Transfer seared pork to a plate, sear onions in the remaining fat, then add water and return pork to pot.

questions.quote: cut mangoes into one inch strips green mangoes
questions.question: How many green mangoes are needed for this soup?
questions.why_it_matters: Green mango is the main acid component; too few leaves it bland, too many makes it intensely sour.

questions.quote: cook the mangoes for about 5 minutes or until it's slightly soft... once the mango is soft after 10 minutes
questions.question: How long should the green mangoes simmer in the broth?
questions.why_it_matters: Overcooking mangoes makes them turn to mush and dissolve completely into the broth.
questions.suggestion: Simmer for 5 to 7 minutes until tender-firm.

questions.quote: test up the chopstick make sure that the chopsticks boiling
questions.question: Can you clarify the chopstick trick for testing the oil heat?
questions.why_it_matters: Searing pork in cold oil will boil the meat in grease rather than creating a brown crust.
questions.suggestion: Place the tip of a dry wooden chopstick into hot oil; when steady bubbles form around it, the oil is hot enough.

questions.quote: start off by making rice you know how to do that
questions.question: What type of rice is typically served with this dish and how much should be prepared?
questions.why_it_matters: The choice of starch completes the meal balance.

notes: Flagged dictation error '10 in yogurt container' for clarification.

questions.question: Do you cool the milk before mixing in the yogurt starter?
questions.why_it_matters: If live yogurt cultures are added to steaming hot milk above 120°F, the heat will kill the bacteria and the yogurt will not set.
questions.suggestion: Cool the milk down to about 110°F (warm to the touch, but not hot) before stirring in the yogurt starter.

questions.question: What brand and size of unflavored yogurt starter do you normally use?
questions.why_it_matters: The transcript says '10 in', which is likely a misheard brand or container size; using the wrong amount or a flavored/pasteurized brand without live cultures will cause fermentation to fail.
questions.suggestion: Use 6 oz to 8 oz of plain, unflavored yogurt with live active cultures (such as Dannon or Fage).

questions.question: What kind of incubator or setting do you use (e.g., yogurt maker, oven with light on, Instant Pot)?
questions.why_it_matters: Yogurt cultures require a steady warm temperature around 105°F–110°F to incubate properly.
questions.suggestion: Use a electric yogurt maker set to 110°F or an Instant Pot on the 'Yogurt' setting.

questions.quote: heat up the milk make sure it doesn't boil uh just until it steams a little bit
questions.question: Do you use a food thermometer to check the milk temperature when heating?
questions.why_it_matters: Scalding milk to around 180°F denatures proteins to yield a thicker yogurt texture without scorching.
questions.suggestion: Heat milk to 180°F over medium-low heat while stirring occasionally.
